There's policies that encourage development in the hamlets, particularly through the plan of subdivision process. There are policies that support communal sanitary systems under certain conditions being established in the township. There's also a policy that is proposing to restrict the number of severances along deficient roads. These are roads that are not up to municipal standard. There's also policies that are supportive of secondary dwelling units, policies to enhance renewable energy development, policies that identify karst topography, which is a natural hazard and limit development near areas known of having karst topography. There's also a new policy section on the Rideau Canal that pulls together a number of policies of the plan. There's clarification of the permitted uses in settlement areas, as well as expanded range of uses on agricultural lands. There's also policies that clarify when a hydrogeologic assessment is required. And there's also a new mapping schedule identifying the elements of the natural heritage system, the wetlands, the woodlands, the ANSIs, and natural corridors that connect those areas. speaker: jeffmckay
text: Hi, thanks. The jurisdiction for telecommunications towers under the Telecommunications Act puts the sole authority for site plan control in, I said, Canada's lap. So the role of the municipality is to really host the municipal and public consultation process that falls underneath the default federal protocol. So if a municipality has a locally enacted telecom protocol that supplements that, then we would follow the procedure of the municipality. Lacking that falls under, strictly under the jurisdiction of what they call the CPC protocol. So it's exempt from, as a federal undertaking, it's exempt from intake and review under Planning Act, any municipal zoning bylaws, any provincial conservation authority, really any level of provincial or municipal government under the authority of parliament. So the municipality's role is to participate in the public consultation process with us to assist us in getting things like the mailing list out and to monitor the process that we use for reply and comment to any public comments received. The duties are all stipulated in the CPC protocol and they require things like newspaper notice for towers over 30 meters. They define the radius that we have to consult with. They define the process that we have to reply when there are public comments received. And at the end of that process, then the municipality is asked for concurrence. So the concurrence is not an approval or a disapproval of the site. What it is is that the municipality is asked to concur that we have followed the governing protocol in completing our duties of public and municipal consultation. So from there, that then goes to ICED or Industry Canada and Industry Canada then makes the decision on approving the site. Okay. So in this case, in both sites, and this is not a surprise, COVID has moved this to front burner that people are desperate to have the internet. And I'm sure you're familiar with the EORN project that there's about $400 million being invested of government money in order to accelerate the rollout of broadband. By 2025, the government's mandate is to be able to deliver high-speed broadband to every resident in the country. And it doesn't matter where they are. So what you'll be seeing is a greater number of these things starting to happen. Rogers is doing, we also do work for Rogers. We're doing 350 towers in the area, basically from Kingston up to Petawawa and then down through the central part. You'll be seeing these towers every probably every four kilometers. Where ExplorNet plays in this business, is there a tier two carrier? So our tier one are Rogers, Telus, Bell. Tier two carriers have smaller antenna loads, smaller data or smaller subscriber requirements. And their strategic initiative and mandate is to fill the coverage gaps that are left between the bigger towers. So historically what's happened is the federal government has a mandate that carriers must, whenever they can, they must share tower facilities. So if Rogers goes in first, they build the tower. And then when Bell wants to come along, they have to prove that they can't use that tower before they can introduce their own tower. And the goal of that was to mitigate the total number of towers that was rolled out. What's happened over the years is that worked when you could get an analog cell call for 20 kilometers. But what's happened is as the technology has gone from HSPA 2G, 3G, 2.5G, 4G, and now into 5G, the coverage radius gets ever smaller as the bandwidth increases. So the good coverage radius on these towers is now only about a kilometer for 5G. So what's happened in the industry is that Rogers and the big guys have built their networks with their towers eight or 10 kilometers apart. And everywhere you've got one of those large towers, the local residents have three or four options for coverage. But now what's happening is that there's no coverage at all and no options whatsoever in the middle space between the existing towers. So ExploreNet and other carriers like them, ExecuLink, ZingDirect, those type of smaller carriers are now filling those spaces by putting the smaller towers basically in the middle.
